text: Earth.
For hundreds of thousands of years,
it has been home to the human species.
By the twenty-first century,
humanity had transformed much of its planet.
Its civilizations had built vast cities,
developed powerful technologies,
and begun exploring the space beyond their atmosphere.
Humanity had long wondered
whether other civilizations existed among the stars.
Few imagined that one had already taken an interest in Earth.
Far beyond the Solar System lay the Hegemony,
an immense interstellar civilization
whose influence extended across numerous star systems.
Its expansion was driven by political ambition,
economic interests, and the continuous demand
for new resources and productive territories.
Earth had attracted its attention.
Earth had already been surveyed,
and the Hegemony had determined that the planet
was a suitable target for expansion.
Its authorities approved the acquisition
and issued a charter to the Sol Development Company.
The Company was given six years
to bring Earth under Hegemony control
and integrate its economy into the wider interstellar system.
An expedition was assembled around
a single interstellar carrier, Caravan,
carrying advanced machinery, industrial equipment,
and the essential components of a future invasion force.
Its destination was the Solar System.
Its objective was Earth.
Caravan sent mining equipment to the asteroid belt.
A small reserve followed,
in case the main workshops were lost.
The workshop packages headed inward.
They arrived between Earth and the Moon,
in a region called cislunar space.
From here, the workshops could supply equipment in Earth orbit.
Shipments of asteroid rock and ice provided the raw materials.
The packages grew into a network of foundries.
Foundry Alpha took ice from asteroids
and turned it into water and propellant.
Foundry Beta refined metal and made beams.
Even the largest frame could cross the distance
to the next workshop in pieces.
At Foundry Gamma, those pieces came together.
A frame made here could carry a precision instrument
brought from another star.
Depots held cargo until the next transfer.
The workshops could keep different schedules.
A fourth branch was called Foundry Delta.
Its precise role remains uncertain.
By now the Company could supply equipment in Earth orbit.
From below, an object arriving there
gave little indication of the industry behind it.
Some of these objects entered human tracking records.
A track could establish where something had been,
and where to look for it again.
What it carried, who had built it,
and why it was there were harder questions.
With ninety days left before contact,
the workshops began handing over finished equipment.
Near Earth, cargo from the Moon’s neighbourhood
began to appear in separate groups in orbit.
Among it were Quivers: disposable dispensers
carrying the glide munitions of the opening Wave.
A tug could spend weeks moving freight.
There was time because the public deadline was still ahead.
Wardens coordinated traffic in orbit.
Far below them, Lanterns sensed and relayed
from the stratosphere.
Asteroids supplied metal.
Compact fusion systems and high-grade seekers
came from home.
At Gamma, another assembly took shape
around precision components drawn from a finite stock.
At an observatory, two exposures might show
a point of light changing position.
The measurement could be sound
while its meaning remained unclear.
The scattered observations never became a warning
governments could act on.
The people comparing them had only pieces of the picture.
Domesday sensors covered selected ground corridors.
Much of the terrain remained unseen.
In the final weeks, the workshops kept working
as more of their output took its place above Earth.
One dispenser had already been set aside for a demonstration.
Its public announcement would come later.
An inert Scythe would give observers a prediction to check.
The event was still ahead.
Nineteen months had passed since the Caravan arrived.
On Earth, the first public word was still to come.
The Company opened a public channel.
This transmission is of nonhuman origin.
Leave military equipment and military structures.
